Piece by piece, he has collected an unusual set of drums from foreign countries. One of them is a clay drum shaped like a vase from Turkey. When he uses it in radio work, he can make it double for an African drum. "In Turkey," Morehouse explained, "the drum is really a duet instrument and is played with a three string mandolin. The mandolin, a long necked instrument, has loose strings which are twanged. The drum is played with the hands and is often heard in hashish houses". Another strange piece which Morehouse insists is classified as a percussion instrument is the jawbone of an ass, painted pink with silver teeth. The sound is achieved by shaking. And the rattling of the teeth produces the sound. The jawbones are used for rhumbas. Morehouse says it is a percussion instrument because a blow is used to make the sound. Two white small drums, mounted on the same stick come from Cuba. They are usually played with the hand on one and a stick on the other. Again, different sounds can be achieved by using different types of sticks. Often they are played with dried gourds. His South African drums are covered with goatskins, even with goat fur. Others are covered with calfskin and pigskin. Morehouse explained the drums vary in Africa as much as do the spoken dialects. There is no set pattern for drums.

A large Chinese tomtom, double headed is being used in a radio studio. 18 inches wide and deep, the sides are made to bulge out in order to stand the strain of the terrific tension of the pigskin covering. The drum is used to attract attention to Chinese theaters, Morehouse explained. He also has two Chinese hand drums mounted on sticks. They are filled with pebble-like pieces and operate like a rattle. The sound is achieved by turning the hand. These instruments are used in festivals and parades. A weirdly pink drum from Haiti is another in Morehouse's collection. A strange one from Indo-China is one of his favorites. Four feet long, the drum doesn't resemble any others. Sound is produced by rubbing a hand over it as with a tambourine. Morehouse explained the drum is used for sending signals because the sound carries only in the direction that the instrument is pointed. The sound. The sound thus travels to its destination without being heard by neighboring villages not in the track of its sound. Morehouse has an engagement to make 12 recordings in which his drum music is featured. Only a few of the drums are in Morehouse's home at 68-41 Ingram Street. The others remain in their radio studios. In spite of Morehouse's growing fame as a drum collector, he is "strictly a dance band man." His own words. He started playing the drums when he was 12.
